problem_description: Return indices of two numbers in an array that add up to target.
user_pseudocode: I will try all pairs using two nested loops
next_steps: Recognize that your nested loop runs in O(n²) time. For n=10,000, that is 100 million operations — too slow to pass time limits.
Reframe the problem: instead of 'find two numbers that sum to target', think 'for each number x, does (target - x) exist in the array?'. This is a lookup, not a search.
Build a hashmap as you iterate: store each number→index. Before inserting x, check if (target-x) is already in the map. If yes, you have your answer in O(1).

problem_description: Return indices of two numbers in an array that add up to target.
user_pseudocode: I will sort the array and then use two pointers from both ends
next_steps: Two pointers on a sorted array finds the pair values in O(n) — great approach. But sorting rearranges positions, so you no longer know the original indices the problem requires.
To preserve indices, store tuples of (value, original_index) before sorting, then apply two pointers on the value field and read indices from the tuple.
Alternatively, skip sorting entirely: a single-pass hashmap stores value→original_index directly and solves the problem in O(n) time without the O(n log n) sorting cost.

problem_description: Return indices of two numbers in an array that add up to target.
user_pseudocode: I will use a hashmap and store number to index as I iterate
next_steps: Before inserting element x into your map, check whether (target - x) is already present. This order ensures you never accidentally use the same element twice.
Handle the edge case mentally: if the same value appears twice and target is 2x, your approach naturally handles it because you check before inserting, so the second occurrence finds the first.
Finalize your return: when complement is found in the map, return [map[target-x], current_index] for the two indices. Your solution is complete at O(n) time and O(n) space.

problem_description: Return indices of two numbers in an array that add up to target.
user_pseudocode: I have no idea where to start
next_steps: Start with the brute force: iterate over every pair (i, j) where i < j and check if nums[i] + nums[j] == target. This guarantees a correct answer even if it is slow.
Now ask: when I am at index i and know nums[i], what exact value am I looking for? The answer is target - nums[i]. This is your complement.
Next ask: do I need to scan the whole array again to find the complement? No — if you remember all numbers you have already seen in a set or map, you can look it up in O(1). Build that map as you go.

problem_description: Check if a bracket string has all brackets correctly matched and nested.
user_pseudocode: I will count opening and closing brackets and check if they are equal
next_steps: Counter-example: '({)}' has 2 opens and 2 closes but is invalid. Equal counts are necessary but not sufficient — you need to verify correct nesting order.
Think about what property makes brackets invalid: a closing bracket that does not match the most recently opened unmatched bracket. You need to track the last unmatched open bracket.
Use a stack: push opening brackets onto it. When you see a closing bracket, pop from the stack and verify the popped bracket matches. After processing the entire string, the stack must be empty.

problem_description: Check if a bracket string has all brackets correctly matched and nested.
user_pseudocode: I will use a stack and push opening brackets, pop and match on closing brackets
next_steps: Handle two critical edge cases: if you encounter a closing bracket but the stack is empty, return False immediately (no matching open bracket exists).
Define a matching map: {')':'(', '}':'{', ']':'['} so you can look up what the corresponding opening bracket should be when checking the stack top.
After the loop, return True only if the stack is empty. A non-empty stack means there are unclosed opening brackets.

problem_description: Check if a bracket string has all brackets correctly matched and nested.
user_pseudocode: I think I need something to track the most recent bracket
next_steps: The data structure you need is a stack: it gives you the most recently pushed item at any time, which is exactly the most recently opened unmatched bracket.

Concretely: iterate the string. If the char is an opening bracket push it. If it is a closing bracket, pop the stack and verify the popped char is the matching opener. If mismatch or stack is empty on pop, return False.
After full iteration, the string is valid if and only if the stack is empty (all opened brackets were matched).

problem_description: Check if a bracket string has all brackets correctly matched and nested.
user_pseudocode: I don't know how to handle three types of brackets at the same time
next_steps: Handle all three bracket types with one simple rule: use a dictionary to map each closing bracket to its expected matching opening bracket: {')':'(', '}':'{', ']':'['}.

Iterate through the string. If a character is an opening bracket push it onto a stack. If it is a closing bracket, look up its expected match in your dictionary, and check if that match equals the current stack top.
If at any point the stack is empty when you expect a match, or the top does not match, return False. Return True at the end only if the stack is empty.

problem_description: Find the length of the longest substring without repeating characters.
user_pseudocode: I will check every substring using two nested loops
next_steps: Checking all substrings is O(n³) with the inner uniqueness check. This approach discards all progress: when you move the left boundary by one, you recheck characters you already processed.
Introduce two pointers defining a window [left, right]. Advance right one step at a time. The window stays valid (no repeats) as long as right can expand. When a repeat is found, shrink from left.
Use a hashmap character→last_seen_index. When s[right] has been seen and its last position is within your window, jump left directly to last_seen[s[right]] + 1, making shrinking O(1) instead of O(n).

problem_description: Find the length of the longest substring without repeating characters.
user_pseudocode: sliding window with left and right pointer, use a set to track chars in window
next_steps: Your approach is correct. One optimization: replace the set with a hashmap (char → last index). When s[right] repeats, instead of moving left one step at a time, jump left to max(left, last_index[s[right]] + 1) instantly.
Always update the hashmap entry for s[right] to right after the check, so future occurrences know the most recent position.
Track max_len = max(max_len, right - left + 1) after each step. This gives O(n) time with a single pass.

problem_description: Find the length of the longest substring without repeating characters.

next_steps: Start by thinking about a window: a contiguous segment of the string defined by a left and right index. Begin with left=0 and right=0.

At each valid step, compute window size as right - left + 1 and update your maximum. This single-pass approach visits each character at most twice.

problem_description: Count distinct ways to climb n stairs taking 1 or 2 steps at a time.
user_pseudocode: I will use recursion to count all paths to step n
next_steps: Your recursive logic is correct: ways(n) = ways(n-1) + ways(n-2). But without caching, you recompute ways(k) exponentially many times, giving O(2^n) time. For n=50 this is computationally infeasible.
Add memoization: store the result of each computed ways(k) in a dictionary. Before recursing, check if the result is already cached. This reduces time to O(n) with O(n) extra space.
Better yet, since each state only depends on the previous two, use two variables and compute iteratively: a, b = 1, 1; for each step compute a, b = b, a+b. This is O(n) time and O(1) space.

problem_description: Count distinct ways to climb n stairs taking 1 or 2 steps at a time.
user_pseudocode: I recognize overlapping subproblems and want to use memoization
next_steps: Memoized recursion is correct and gives O(n) time. You can also do this bottom-up with a dp array: dp[0]=1, dp[1]=1, then dp[i]=dp[i-1]+dp[i-2] for i from 2 to n.
Space-optimize further: since dp[i] only depends on dp[i-1] and dp[i-2], two variables are enough. Let a, b = dp[i-2], dp[i-1] and update at each step.
Set your base cases carefully: ways(0)=1 (one way to stand at bottom and do nothing), ways(1)=1, ways(2)=2. Your loop should run from index 2 through n inclusive.

problem_description: Count distinct ways to climb n stairs taking 1 or 2 steps at a time.
user_pseudocode: I think it is permutations or combinations of 1s and 2s
next_steps: Combinatorics gets complicated here because the number of 1s and 2s in each path varies. Think recursively instead: to reach step n, your last move was either from step n-1 or n-2.
This means ways(n) = ways(n-1) + ways(n-2). Write out small cases: ways(1)=1, ways(2)=2, ways(3)=3, ways(4)=5. Do you recognize this sequence? It is Fibonacci.
Now implement it iteratively: start with two variables representing the last two values and update them in a loop up to n. No recursion, no memoization dictionary, just two variables.

problem_description: Reverse a singly linked list in-place and return the new head.
user_pseudocode: I will collect all values in an array then recreate the list in reverse
next_steps: Collecting values and recreating uses O(n) extra space and creates new nodes instead of reversing the existing ones. Try reversing the actual next pointers in-place.
Introduce two pointers: prev=None and curr=head. Your goal: make each curr.next point to prev instead of forward.
The pointer reversal loop is: save nxt=curr.next (so you don't lose the chain), set curr.next=prev, then advance prev=curr and curr=nxt. Repeat until curr is None. Return prev as the new head.

problem_description: Reverse a singly linked list in-place and return the new head.
user_pseudocode: I will use prev and curr pointers but I need to save next before changing curr.next
next_steps: You have the core insight. The exact four-line reversal body is: (1) nxt = curr.next, (2) curr.next = prev, (3) prev = curr, (4) curr = nxt.
Initialize: prev = None, curr = head. Your loop condition is while curr is not None.
After the loop, curr is None and prev points to the old tail, which is now the new head. Return prev.

problem_description: Reverse a singly linked list in-place and return the new head.
user_pseudocode: I don't know the order of pointer operations
next_steps: Trace through a small example: 1→2→3→None. After reversal you want 3→2→1→None. Start at node 1 with prev=None. You want to make 1 point to None (prev). But first save node 2 so you can continue.
The order that works: temp=curr.next (save forward link), curr.next=prev (flip pointer), prev=curr (advance prev), curr=temp (advance curr using saved forward link).
After processing all three nodes, curr=None and prev=node 3 which is the new head. Return prev.

problem_description: Find the index of target in a sorted array in O(log n). Return -1 if not found.
user_pseudocode: I will scan every element from left to right
next_steps: Linear scan is O(n) and ignores the sorted property entirely. The problem requires O(log n) which means you must eliminate half the search space at each step.
Use two pointers: left=0 and right=len(arr)-1. Compute mid=(left+right)//2 and compare arr[mid] to target.
If arr[mid] < target, target must be in the right half, so set left=mid+1. If arr[mid] > target, set right=mid-1. If equal, return mid. Repeat while left <= right.

problem_description: Find the index of target in a sorted array in O(log n). Return -1 if not found.
user_pseudocode: I will use left and right pointers and compare the middle element
next_steps: Lock in your loop invariant: while left <= right (using <= not <) ensures you examine a single-element range when left and right converge.
Update correctly: when moving left, use left=mid+1 (not mid) and when moving right use right=mid-1 (not mid). Using mid instead would create an infinite loop when left==right.
After the loop exits with no match, return -1. Your algorithm is now O(log n) time and O(1) space.

problem_description: Find the index of target in a sorted array in O(log n). Return -1 if not found.
user_pseudocode: I know the sorted property is useful but I don't know how to use it
next_steps: Sorted order means: all elements left of index i are smaller than arr[i], and all elements right are larger. Use this to cut search space in half.
Look at the middle element arr[mid]. If arr[mid] == target you are done. If arr[mid] < target, you know target cannot be in the left half, so discard it by setting left=mid+1.
Each comparison eliminates half the remaining candidates. With n=1024 elements this means at most 10 comparisons. This is O(log n).

problem_description: Merge nums2 into nums1 in-place. nums1 has m+n size with trailing zeros for n elements of nums2.
user_pseudocode: I will put all elements in one array and sort it
next_steps: Concatenate and sort is O((m+n)log(m+n)) and wastes the fact that both inputs are already sorted. A proper merge should run in O(m+n).
Merging from the front is dangerous: you would overwrite unread elements of nums1. The trick is to fill from the back where the trailing zeros are.

Place three pointers: p1=m-1 (last real element of nums1), p2=n-1 (last element of nums2), p=m+n-1 (write position). Each step, place the larger of nums1[p1] or nums2[p2] at nums1[p] and decrement the appropriate pointers.

problem_description: Merge nums2 into nums1 in-place. nums1 has m+n size with trailing zeros for n elements of nums2.
user_pseudocode: fill from back using three pointers comparing last elements of each array
next_steps: Your loop: while p2 >= 0: if p1 >= 0 and nums1[p1] > nums2[p2]: nums1[p]=nums1[p1]; p1-=1 else: nums1[p]=nums2[p2]; p2-=1; p-=1
You only need to continue the loop while p2 >= 0. If p2 reaches -1 first, all remaining nums1 elements are already in the correct positions.
If p1 reaches -1 first, the remaining nums2 elements are already smaller than anything in nums1, and the else branch copies them correctly. Your solution handles all cases in O(m+n) time O(1) space.

problem_description: Find the contiguous subarray with the largest sum and return its sum.
user_pseudocode: I will check every possible subarray and track the maximum sum
next_steps: O(n²) or O(n³) approaches recompute partial sums from scratch. A key observation: when extending a subarray, if the running total has gone negative, starting fresh is always better for future elements.
At each element make a local decision: current_sum = max(num, current_sum + num). This means: if extending hurts (current_sum is negative), start fresh from this element.
Track max_sum = max(max_sum, current_sum) after each update. Initialize both with nums[0] to handle all-negative arrays. This is Kadane's algorithm: O(n) time O(1) space.

problem_description: Find the contiguous subarray with the largest sum and return its sum.
user_pseudocode: running sum and reset when negative, track best
next_steps: When resetting, set current_sum to the current element (not 0). Resetting to 0 would incorrectly skip the current element itself, and would fail on all-negative inputs.
The update is: current_sum = max(nums[i], current_sum + nums[i]). This captures both choices: start new subarray at i, or extend the existing one.
Initialize current_sum = nums[0] and max_sum = nums[0] before the loop. Iterate from index 1. This handles the constraint that the subarray must be non-empty.

problem_description: Return true if any value appears at least twice in nums.
user_pseudocode: I will compare all pairs of elements
next_steps: O(n²) pair comparison is too slow for large inputs. Instead of checking all pairs, think about the problem as: have I seen this number before in a single forward pass?
A Python set supports O(1) average add and in-membership test. Create an empty set and iterate: if the current number is already in the set, return True; otherwise add it.
If you complete the loop without returning True, no duplicate was found: return False. This is O(n) time and O(n) space in the worst case.

problem_description: Return true if any value appears at least twice in nums.
user_pseudocode: sort first then adjacent comparison
next_steps: Sorting + adjacent check is O(n log n) time O(1) space. It modifies the array, which may matter in some contexts. Confirm whether in-place sorting is acceptable.
The hash set approach is O(n) time O(n) space and does not modify the array. For very memory-constrained environments sorting is better; for speed the set is better.
If you use sorting, the check is: for i in range(1, len(nums)): if nums[i]==nums[i-1]: return True. Return False after the loop.
